title: Apple foldable iPhone: New boss starts with gamble on £1,999 device
description: Apple has launched its most expensive iPhone ever - a foldable handheld that costs at least £1,999 and marks the first major iPhone design change in a
body: Apple has launched its most expensive iPhone ever - a foldable handheld that costs at least £1,999 and marks the first major iPhone design change in almost 20 years.The iPhone Duo is a gamble by new boss John Ternus, who took over from long-time chief executive Tim Cook this month. Apple is entering the foldable phone market comparatively late, following the likes of South Korea's Samsung and China's Huawei. Ternus told an audience at Apple's California headquarters: "Others have created foldables that just feel like two phones awkwardly stuck together." Apple's model, he claimed "redefine[s] the experience of using a foldable phone".In the US, prices start at $1,999, but can go up to $3,200. It has taken eight years to develop, something Ternus was directly involved in after spending many years as a top executive inside Apple's hardware division.When unfolded, it looks like a small iPad and a wider iPhone when it is folded.Ternus said: "It's entirely new and at the same time remarkably familiar. A similar size to your passport, it feels familiar to hold and comfortable to use with one hand."But the product is facing established competitors. "The real fight is China, where Huawei owns nearly 80% of foldables." said Francisco Jeronimo, vice president for data and analytics, devices at IDC EMEA.Ben Wood, chief analyst at technology research firm FDM CCS Insight, said it was likely Ternus's promotion was timed specifically "to coincide with what will be arguably one of the biggest iPhone launches for many years"."Nothing happens by accident at Apple," he said.Carolina Milanesi, an analyst at Creative Strategies who attended the Wednesday presentation, said the spotlight on Ternus made it feel "almost like he was a product himself." Altering the design of the iPhone may address some criticism that Apple has yet to land a major product hit or truly exciting innovation since the first iPhone came out in 2007."The foldable risks becoming a premium-priced ornament in the portfolio, imparting badge value but not meaningful growth," said Dipanjan Chatterjee, an analyst at Forrester.Previously, the highest starting price of the newest iPhone was $900 (£664).Apple also revealed on Wednesday the new iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max, which in the US start at $1,199 and $1,299 respectively. Chatterjee said the foldable iPhone could go the way of Apple's Vision Pro headset, which the company priced at $3,699 and has not been a hit with buyers.Or, he said, it could be the company's next Apple Watch which, while not as popular as the iPhone, is bought by millions of people each year.The way people have become accustomed to the way the iPhone operates is another potential hurdle to Apple seeing big sales of the new design."Foldables are interesting devices", Milanesi noted. "A lot of people are intrigued by it, but the software and the learning curve that you have from moving from a traditional phone to a foldable is real."Wood noted that the current market for foldable smartphones from the likes of Samsung and Huawei make up only 2% of smartphone sales. Even with Apple's version likely driving interest and demand, sales are only expected to reach 4% of the total market in the next decade, according to data and analytics firm FDM CCM Insight.The iPhone has been Apple's top-selling product and accounts for more than half of the company's sales each year.In recent quarters, the company has boasted that the iPhone is more in-demand than ever, with the most recent version of the device becoming its most successful product launch.The company also revealed more about the coming relaunch of its audio and chat assistant Siri, which it now calls Siri AI.Starting with the iPhone 18, the bot will now be able to go across information on a person's phone, like messages and emails, to find information, answer queries and take action on a person's behalf.Some Siri AI features will also be available on the new Apple Watch, including the ability to take notes of conversations and transcribe them, should a wearer enable that feature.Ternus referred to new AI-enabled capabilities on the iPhone as an "intelligent personal hub", and admitted that Apple would be making use of "the most private details of your daily life."He insisted that all of it will remain private, with the AI features often running "on device", meaning not through third-party companies. And when a third-party is required for a function, Ternus said it will remain private in a remote server, or cloud."Others see that data as something to collect and store", Ternus said. "Here, not even Apple can access what's yours."

schema.headline: Apple foldable iPhone: New boss starts with gamble on £1,999 device

title: Uganda's King Oyo death: Royal family rejects UBC presenter Edward Rukidi Kijanangoma as the new monarch
description: "My brother did leave behind an heir to the throne, and that was very clearly stated," she said, accusing those behind the announcement on Wednesday n
body: "My brother did leave behind an heir to the throne, and that was very clearly stated," she said, accusing those behind the announcement on Wednesday night of creating "confusion and turmoil" while the family was still grieving.Meanwhile the late king's mother, Queen Best Kemigisa, has said royal guards have been withdrawn from the palace and soldiers deployed, restricting the royal family's movement and their ability to receive visitors, describing the situation as "house arrest".She appealed to the army's leadership and President Yoweri Museveni to allow the family to mourn and bury Oyo in peace on Saturday."I appeal to those fighting over the throne: please, there will be time for all of that," she said. "Let us grieve and bury my son King Oyo."Thousands of mourners are expected to attend the burial at the royal tombs near the palace in Fort Portal in western Uganda.His body was returned to Uganda from the US on Friday, and preparations for the funeral are under way.Tooro is one of Uganda's traditional kingdoms. Its monarch has no formal political authority but remains an important cultural figure in western Uganda.Uganda abolished its traditional kingdoms in 1967, but they were restored in the 1990s under President Museveni. Their monarchs are recognised as cultural leaders rather than political rulers.The existence of Oyo's son was first publicly revealed in the days after the king's death by President Museveni, who said he had been told about the young boy by the queen mother.No other details have officially been disclosed, and he had not previously been presented as Oyo's heir.The disagreement has exposed the complicated way in which succession works in Tooro.Unlike Britain's monarchy, where the crown passes according to an established line of succession, Tooro's monarch is chosen from the Babiito, the royal dynastic clan.At a press conference in ​the kingdom's capital of Fort Portal, the royal clan's succession committee announced Kijanangoma, Oyo's cousin and a news presenter ​at the state-run broadcaster UBC, as monarch.The clan elders said they had the customary authority to choose a suitable prince to become "the Omukama" - the local title for the king of Tooro.The succession panel said it had carried out "due diligence, consultation and adequate consideration" before selecting Kijanangoma, with 19 members signing the resolution. Kijanangoma is the son of Prince Christopher Paul Kijanangoma and a grandson of former Tooro king George David Rukidi III.Another contender had been Prince George Desmond Kamurasi - a footballer for one of the best-known amateur clubs in the UK. According to the succession committee, the South East Dons captain and goalkeeper declined the offer of the throne, citing other responsibilities.It is not yet clear when the enthronement will take place, but the committee said it would be conducted in accordance with the traditions and customs of the Tooro kingdom.

schema.headline: Uganda's King Oyo death: Royal family rejects UBC presenter Edward Rukidi Kijanangoma as the new monarch

title: Iran war won't end until after US midterm elections, says Trump
description: US President Donald Trump has said he does not think the Iran war will end until after November's midterm elections, adding that oil prices will not c
body: US President Donald Trump has said he does not think the Iran war will end until after November's midterm elections, adding that oil prices will not come down until then."I think the war's going to end immediately after the election because they can't hold out any longer," Trump said of Iran's leaders on Wednesday.He made the comments as he headed to Texas for the Republican Party's first midterm election convention – and repeated them there, arguing that short-term economic pain was worth it to prevent Iran from developing nuclear weapons.Trump is facing falling polling numbers and pressure from within his party to end the war, which began when the US and Israel attacked Iran in February.The conflict rapidly spread across the Middle East, as Iran retaliated by launching missiles and drones at Israel and Arab states hosting US military facilities.The price of Brent crude oil, the global benchmark, has risen above the $100 (£74) mark three times over the past six months, with Iranian attacks forcing production stoppages in Gulf states and disrupting exports through the vital Strait of Hormuz waterway.The US has also imposed a naval blockade on Iran's ports and has recently begun striking Iranian tankers in response to attacks on warships and other vessels."Right after the election, oil prices are going to be tumbling downward," Trump told reporters. "I think it's going to take a little bit longer than the midterm."He added that Iran was "desperate to try and affect the election, so that we can get a nice weak group of people in there" – an apparent reference to the Democrats – "and leave them alone and let them have their nuclear weapon".He provided no proof of the election claim. Tehran has repeatedly denied it is seeking nuclear weapons and insisted its nuclear programme is solely peaceful.At the convention in Texas, Trump echoed some of these lines, saying the price of oil would tumble "as soon as we win the war with Iran".In his speech, he also referenced dissatisfaction among some Americans on the issue: "Guys come up to me and say, 'I wish you didn't do the war in Iran. Now gasoline is up'".Trump also said further negotiations with Iran could possibly happen, "but it's not something we're looking at".The US president initially predicted the war, which is now in its seventh month, would last only a matter of weeks. The conflict, and its knock-on effects on everything from fuel to groceries, has led to a steep decline in his approval ratings – and pressure from those within his party, including staunch supporters, to quickly end the war.Midterm elections will be held on 3 November, and Republicans are in danger of losing control on Congress.At the convention, Trump sought to energise the party ahead of November. Historically, a sitting president's party tends to lose seats in Congress in the midterm elections.Fighting in the Middle East has intensified in recent days, as oil facilities throughout the region come under attack, driving up the global price of fuel and other goods that require shipping.The price of oil hit $100 a barrel on Wednesday for the first time since July. Similarly, earlier this week the price of US diesel hit an all-time high, which is likely to cause a ripple effect on prices across the US.There are also predictions that the rising fuel costs could lead to higher interest rates.On Tuesday night, the US military said it had attacked and destroyed five oil tankers with ties to Iran's Islamic Revolution Guard Corps (IRGC) in the Gulf of Oman and the northern Gulf.The IRGC, in response, said early on Wednesday that its naval forces had attacked two US Navy destroyers and eight oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz, causing "heavy damage" to the vessels. Centcom denied its warships were hit.The IRGC also said it had launched ballistic missiles at US military maintenance facilities, hangars and aircraft at Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan.Jordan's armed forces said they intercepted 20 Iranian missiles and that two other missiles fell in unpopulated areas with no casualties reported.Later on Wednesday, sources told CBS News, the BBC's US partner, that several US fighter jets at the air base were damaged in the Iranian strikes.One A-10 Thunderbolt aircraft was hit and was missing a wing, and about eight F-15s sustained light damage, according to people familiar with the matter.Explosions were reported in southern Iran on Wednesday night, but Iranian official sources denied they were US strikes, saying the sounds came from the sea.In a separate development on Tuesday, the Iran-backed Houthi movement in Yemen launched a wave of missile and drone attacks on south-western Saudi Arabia, the world's largest oil exporter, causing fires at several oil facilities.Saudi media reported more Houthi attacks on the kingdom on Wednesday, citing a military spokesman as condemning missile and drone strikes on the cities of Khamis Mushait, Abha and Jazan.The Houthis have said they are retaliating for days of Saudi air strikes on their territory in western Yemen, where a four-year-old informal ceasefire has collapsed.

schema.headline: Iran war won't end until after US midterm elections, says Trump

title: Muted US response to UK's West Bank sanctions may reflect simmering frustration
description: As the UK unveiled sanctions against Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank on Tuesday, Israel responded with fury, declaring it would shutter
body: As the UK unveiled sanctions against Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank on Tuesday, Israel responded with fury, declaring it would shutter Britain's diplomatic mission to the Palestinians, kick out UK military staff from an international coordination base near Gaza and ban nearly a dozen left-wing British members of parliament from entering Israel.It was a blaring signal of defiance and a remarkable diplomatic escalation. The UK had taken the action arguing it had a moral imperative to stop the "destruction" of the two-state solution - a future independent Palestinian state - at the hands of the Israeli government. It accused Israel's government of turning a blind eye to the "ethnic cleansing" of Palestinians by settlers.The standoff, which by the afternoon extended to a further 11 mostly European countries set to join the settlement trade ban, raised a crucial question: When Israel becomes isolated, the US as its superpower backer often steps in to provide a diplomatic shield. Was the US, too, going to condemn Britain's policy?Such a reprimand had been previewed by some observers. It felt even more likely when the US ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, appeared on the BBC before the UK announcement suggesting American "sanctions, repercussions or retaliations" could be coming for Britain, albeit that he didn't know what these were and hadn't spoken to President Trump.But as Tuesday wore on, Washington's response was notably muted. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, asked about the UK move by reporters on the way to Colombia, said: "Obviously, we're not going to do what the UK did. We saw their announcement today but I don't have any comment on it right now." He added that Britain had notified the administration ahead of time (most likely during a phone call Trump had with UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham on Monday) and said the US shared "the goal of stability" at a tense time in the region and didn't "want to see some uptick in violence… in the West Bank". It was hardly a withering rebuke of the British move, let alone any kind of punishment. In fact, Washington seemed to be sharing some of the concerns that motivated the move.Asked about it on Wednesday, Trump said he would be speaking to Israel to understand their thinking, adding: "I understand exactly what's going on, but I want to find out why all of a sudden has that happened."My understanding is that discussions about the US response were taking place at a high level within the administration on Tuesday. The baseline position appeared to be against any moves that could negatively impact American companies. Huckabee, who has longstanding views based on biblical justifications for Jewish settlement in the West Bank, appeared to be speaking off the cuff in some of his public remarks - a feature now common for some Trump-appointed ambassadors. Staunchly pro-Israel Republicans in Congress were very publicly arguing for actions against Britain; pointing out that US states like Florida have punitive laws against companies that boycott Israel. But from the White House and State Department, more targeted criticism of the UK did not materialise.It is still possible the administration will come out with some condemnation of the British move in the coming days. But the lack of any urgent pushback is likely to reflect current frustrations within the Trump administration at the Israeli leadership. Trump's biggest foreign policy priority currently is trying to prevent the crisis worsening in the Strait of Hormuz, now the focal point of his stalemated war with Iran. His joint attack with the Israelis has left numerous friction points in his complex relationship with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. At critical moments when Trump tried to reach a deal with Tehran, Netanyahu escalated fighting against Hezbollah in Lebanon. Israel has said it was acting against threats to security, but the moves had the potential to derail US diplomacy. Meanwhile, Trump wants progress on his Gaza peace initiative, involving disarmament of Hamas and Israeli military withdrawal. Netanyahu has publicly rejected the plan in its current formulation.Officially, the State Department referred me to Rubio's comments in Miami in relation to the UK announcement. But all told, Trump appears unwilling to come out to bat for Netanyahu currently. This has extended to him so far not endorsing Netanyahu in the upcoming Israeli election. The administration, aware of splits within Trump's base of support on Israel, has also itself grown irritated at the extent of settler violence in the West Bank, given the lack of action by the Israeli government to meaningfully punish it. This is embarrassing for the White House. West Bank violence against Palestinians is frequently the subject of protests from Trump's Gulf Arab allies - the countries mediating on Gaza, who Trump needs to pressure Hamas. They wonder how the US can draw concessions from the Israelis in relation to this if it can't on settler violence in the West Bank. Trump eyes a legacy prize in both defeating Iran and moving forward with his Gaza peace plan - so batting for Israel against Europe over West Bank settlements seems to be, for Trump - so far, at least - juice that is not worth the squeeze.

schema.headline: Muted US response to UK's West Bank sanctions may reflect simmering frustration

title: NFL in Melbourne: Can American football win Australians over?
description: American football is coming to Australia - can it succeed?Image source, Supplied: San Francisco 49ersImage caption, George Kittle of the San Francisco
body: American football is coming to Australia - can it succeed?Image source, Supplied: San Francisco 49ersImage caption, George Kittle of the San Francisco 49ers and other players were greeted by fans in Melbourne this weekBySimon AtkinsonAustralia producerAn oval ball, in September, in Melbourne usually means just one thing - the business end of the Australian rules football (AFL) season.But on Friday, at the unsportingly early time of 7am, 100,000 people will begin filing into the Melbourne Cricket Ground (MCG) for a very un-Australian sporting spectacle - American football.The LA Rams take on the San Francisco 49ers in their opening National Football League (NFL) fixture, the first time the country has hosted a meaningful, non-exhibition regular season game.The match sold out months ago, with more than half the crowd expected to be people living outside the state of Victoria. On the official ticket resale site, a restricted view seat is priced at more than A$650 (£350/US$470)."Walking down the street, it's AFL finals week and you wouldn't even know," says Thomas McMillan, host of the NFL podcast Any Given Sunday Australia."It's all NFL everywhere. There are bars that are nothing but 49ers bars or Rams bars. We have a Ram Tram getting around the district. When you're in Melbourne and AFL isn't visible, it shows how big this is at the moment."Kickoff at 10.35am local time on Friday may not be typical for local fans, but meets the demands of prime time US television schedules and their advertisers.The league held its first international match in 2007, and over the past two decades the overseas matches have become a long-term strategy to attract supporters and their dollars.Nine games outside the US are scheduled for the upcoming season, including three in London. But Melbourne is the furthest that players and US-based fans will have to travel.Image source, Supplied: LA RamsImage caption, Fans admire an LA Rams mural in a Melbourne laneway"Obviously there are question marks when you hear you are playing in Australia," 49ers running back Christian McCaffrey told a press conference this week."But it has been so cool… the food's incredible, the coffee's great."That caffeine reference was perhaps as much to the time zone, as nod to the city's famous café culture.Melbourne is a mind-warping 17 hours ahead of California where both teams are based, and much of the pre-match attention has been on the two teams and their contrasting approaches to trying to "beat" the jet lag.For the 49ers, who arrived late last week, their players have had time to get over the long journey, adjust to the time zone, acclimatise and practice at a nearby stadium.Controversially, the LA Rams are taking things to the other extreme, planning to arrive on Thursday morning local time on a chartered Qantas A380 superjumbo, play on Friday, and get back to the US west coast shortly afterwards, in theory to prepare for their next match with minimum disruption to the player's body clocks."Definitely it's a gamble," says McMillan. "If they don't quite get things right after the 16-hour flight, you still might have that jet lag, even though you're trying to avoid it.""And not everyone can sleep on planes," says his co-host Danny Webb. "Whether you're in first class, business class, whatever it is, you're still on a plane.""And", adds McMillan: "And they're six foot six most of them, so it's going to be even tighter seats".Despite it technically being a "home" game for the Rams, who bid for NFL marketing rights in Australia under the leagues Global Markets programme, this all means it is the San Francisco 49ers that have more of a presence around Melbourne this week.Image source, Supplied: San Francisco 49ersImage caption, Former NFL players Joe Nedney (left) and Jesse Sapolu attend a "sausage sizzle"And while most practice sessions have been behind closed doors, there have been player appearances at a rally for fans and an AFL match, while ex-stars turned up at that most Australian of traditions, the weekly fundraising "sausage sizzle" at the country's most high-profile hardware chain.American sports journalist Dontay Atkinson predicts this fan engagement will be reflected inside the stadium and that the MCG will be "heavily red" (the 49ers colour), accusing the Rams of doing  "exactly jack squat to sell the NFL brand or connect with Australians".Writing on X he added: "Fly in, fly out, no contact. I'm sure the Aussies feel great about that snub."McMillan says he can understand the approach by the Rams, who are seen as contenders for the 2027 Superbowl."They're looking at this as a game they need to win," he says."We do feel a bit snubbed, and feel the 49ers are doing the right thing,"But it is their job, so that's where the Rams coaching staff has gone 'nah, we're taking this approach'."I just worry that they have missed the boat of ingraining themselves as the Australian team. It leaves it open for others, and the 49ers have really jumped on that."Image source, Supplied: San Francisco 49ersImage caption, Cheerleaders for the San Francisco 49ers dance in Melbourne's Federation SquareThe LA Rams insist there has been no snub, though speaking to the BBC, the club's Head of International Stephanie Cheng dodged the question of whether she would have preferred her players to have been in town this week."It's really a culmination of more than four years of work," she said. "It's not just about game week. We have long term rights."Cheng says the Rams are the only NFL team with a membership programme for Australian fans, and that it has sent coaches into schools and communities to promote "flag football" – the non-contact version of the sport which will feature in the LA 2028 Olympics.She also points to regular earlier visits by star players including running back Kyren Williams in March. This week its cheerleaders have visited US military bases in Australia before coming to Melbourne, and the franchise has installed a 22-yard floating football field on Melbourne's Yarra River serving as a fan zone."From day one, when we've come to Australia, there's been incredible enthusiasm," Cheng said.While no Australian players will be on the field on Friday, there are dozens playing US college football and a handful in the NFL.Most are punters, kicking specialists tapped up after showing their prowess playing AFL or rugby league.But it is the success of Jordan Mailata, an offensive left tackle with the Philadelphia Eagles, who in 2025 became the first Australian to play in, and win, a Superbowl that was a "major turning point in Australia's fandom of the NFL " says Webb."Seeing an Australian in what we'd called a skilled position and then winning a Superbowl. It doesn't get better than that".Friday's game is the first of three matches in Melbourne to be held over four years, under a contract between the NFL and the state of Victoria.Image source, Supplied: LA RamsImage caption, The LA Rams hosted a community day for American football fans in the run-up to the Melbourne matchThe league's preference, says Gerrit Meier, managing director and head of NFL International, is to have annual games in Australia similar, to the way the game has grown in the UK."We're working off the hypothesis that we need to make a commitment to a market," he told Reuters.And while many US-based supporters are not fans of the international fixtures, these games are here to stay, says Webb, and the hype and the sell-out crowd in Australia augurs well for it to become a long-term fixture,"I had mates four years ago asking why are you doing an NFL podcast? It's not a big sport here," he said."And now every single one of those mates are asking me for tickets for the game."

schema.headline: NFL in Melbourne: Can American football win Australians over?

title: Four takeaways from Trump's speech at midterms convention
description: Four key takeaways from  Republican midterms conventionFigure caption, Watch: Trump tells supporters their vote will decide if country "stumbles" or "
body: Four key takeaways from  Republican midterms conventionFigure caption, Watch: Trump tells supporters their vote will decide if country "stumbles" or "moves forward"ByDaniel Bush Washington correspondent, reporting from Dallas The Republican Party's first midterms convention had all the trappings of the traditional presidential election-year gathering: supporters in sparkling costumes, a conveyor belt of candidate speeches, and vendors selling campaign merchandise.But unlike an ordinary convention, no official party business was conducted in Dallas, with the event instead serving as a rally for Republicans who are seeking to boost turnout and avoid losing control of Congress in November.President Donald Trump, whose grip over the party remains absolute, delivered a lengthy keynote speech on Wednesday during the opening night of the two-day event. He covered many of the subjects he has returned to time and again this year - with a few surprises thrown in.Here are the key takeaways from his address.1. Preaching to the MAGA choirThe vast arena was filled with diehard Trump supporters sporting red MAGA gear from his past presidential campaigns. A decade after his first White House run, Trump is still beloved among his base and he has bent the party to his will in the years since.The old-style Republican establishment, or what's left of it in the Trump era, was nowhere to be seen. Senator Susan Collins of Maine and other Republicans running in competitive races chose to stay away. Image source, Getty ImagesThe absence of more moderate Republicans was glaring and offered a reminder of just how much the party has changed.It also raised questions about the effectiveness of holding an unprecedented midterm convention in the first place. The core audience, both in the arena and watching on television, appeared to be Trump loyalists, not the moderates and swing voters the Republican Party needs to turn out in large numbers in November.2. Trump offers $5,000 payoutFigure caption, Watch: Trump says US adults will get $5,000 if Republicans win midtermsTrump has long thrown out unconventional ideas at rallies. On Wednesday night, that came in the form of an offer to pay every adult US citizen $5,000 (£3,700) if Republicans win both chambers of Congress in November.The only caveat, Trump said, was the money would have to be spent in the US.He offered no details on how the plan would work, where the money would come from, or how the US government would monitor how it was spent. Democrats quickly labelled it an "empty promise" and others questioned whether such a pledge was even legal.There are nearly 270 million American adults, which means a $5,000 payout would cost the US government some $1.3 trillion.Whether the plan was possible or not appeared to be beside the point. The idea drew raucous applause at the convention and Trump seemed to relish the moment.3. A gamble on affordabilityEarlier on Wednesday, as he departed for the convention, Trump acknowledged that Americans may have to wait a while longer to see relief from high fuel prices."I think it's going to take a little bit longer than the midterms," Trump said.The president reiterated that message in his speech, arguing that short-term economic pain caused by the war in Iran was worth it to prevent Tehran from developing nuclear weapons.But that may be a difficult message to land with voters who are feeling higher prices.Figure caption, Watch: Do Republicans blame Trump for high oil prices?Polls have consistently indicated in recent months that the cost of living is a top-ranking issue among Americans.Trump's approval rating, too, has taken a hit as the war in Iran has dragged on. A Financial Times / Focaldata poll released on Sunday indicated that it had hit a new low, with only 33% of registered voters approving of his presidential performance.Many Republican candidates may well have hoped for a more direct message on addressing the cost of living and quickly ending the war in Iran.4. It's still Trump's party Trump's total grip on the party raises some pointed questions about its future. Namely - who will replace him? And more immediately for November's elections, how will it perform when his name isn't on the ballot?Image source, Getty ImagesTrump offered a simple solution to the latter question on Wednesday night. After warning that the sitting president tends to lose the midterms, he told the crowd: "I'm asking you to pretend that I'm on the ballot."The remark was an acknowledgement by Trump that he remains the party's best driver of turnout. It also speaks to the challenge Republicans have both in November and in the next presidential election in 2028.Trump will not be on the ballot again, and though he can continue campaigning for the party, there is not a clear or obvious successor who can rally the base quite like Trump.In interviews with the BBC, convention goers often looked ahead to the election in two years' time and debated who Trump's successor should be. Vice-President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio were frequently mentioned as top contenders.Trump, however, made clear in Dallas that he is still in charge and is not in a hurry to give up the spotlight.Follow the twists and turns of Trump's second term with North America correspondent Anthony Zurcher's weekly US Politics Unspun newsletter. Readers in the UK can sign up here. Those outside the UK can sign up here.

schema.headline: Four takeaways from Trump's speech at midterms convention

title: Five dead and 86 missing as fire breaks out on ferry in the Philippines
description: Figure caption, Watch: What we know about the fatal Philippines ferry fireByVirma Simonette RiveraReporting fromManila and Kelly NgUpdated 9 hours ago
body: Figure caption, Watch: What we know about the fatal Philippines ferry fireByVirma Simonette RiveraReporting fromManila and Kelly NgUpdated 9 hours agoAt least five people have died and 86 are missing after a fire broke out on a ferry in the Philippines, the country's coastguard said.The MV June Aster, which set off from Manila ferrying 117 passengers and 17 crew members, was nearing its destination at the tourist hotspot of Coron when it caught fire.The blaze, which erupted at 18:45 local time (10:45 GMT) Wednesday, was still burning as of 11:00 on Thursday. The strong currents and thick smoke were a challenge to those working to extinguish it, the coastguard said.A survivor said he floated in the sea for two hours before he got rescued. "It was cold. If the rescue had been delayed, I would definitely have died," Roland Lerma told the BBC. Image source, Philippine Coast GuardImage caption, The fire broke out as the vessel was reaching the tourist hotspot of Coron in PalawanVideo clips shared by the coastguard on Wednesday night showed the vessel engulfed in flames and people being pulled out of the water into rescue boats.The cause of the fire remains under investigation, the coastguard said.The coastguard said preliminary interviews with the survivors suggest the fire started in the cargo hold, which is the compartment where containers and or goods are stored, the coastguard said. Some passengers were not wearing life vests, they noted.Forty-three people have been rescued but it is unclear how many have sustained injuries. Seven of the survivors were taken to a hospital in Culion, a larger neighbouring island, which has higher bed capacity and more comprehensive healthcare services.A first responder told the BBC they had never seen such a disaster in Coron, calling it "really heartbreaking". "I was one of the people who carried and transported the casualties to the hospital last night," they said, adding that the ferry was an hour away from its destination.The survivors were taken to an evacuation centre in Barangay Turda, which sits just north of Marcilla. The state of their injuries is unclear.Image source, ReutersImage caption, Footage from the coastguard show the vessel engulfed in flamesRai Garcia has three family friends among those missing.Mae Lorraine Galera-Navoa, who is the sister of Garcia's brother-in-law, had travelled to Luzon to attend her father's funeral, accompanied by her husband Elyzer Navoa and their three-year-old daughter Hiraya Joy.They had been travelling home to El Nido in Palawan on board the vessel when it caught fire."We haven't received any news yet. That's why we had to comment on local news threads just to receive updates," Garcia says."We still hope and pray for their safety." Garcia and his family made a poster to appeal for information of the family of three using a photo Mae had taken on the ferry and shared with immediate relatives.Others have posted on the Philippine Coast Guard's Facebook page asking for information of their missing loved ones. "Please can you find my sibling," read one comment.Maritime accidents are common in the Philippines, an archipelago of 7,100 islands.Inter-island ferries are a cheap way to move people and cargo between islands, some of which are inaccessible by air.But there is always the risk of severe weather, monsoon rains and typhoons which can cause turbulent conditions. The country is affected by an average of 20 typhoons every year.Past accidents have also been blamed on poor maintenance and uneven enforcement of safety laws.In 2023, 31 people died after a fire broke out at a passenger ferry in the country's south-western tip. The MV Lady Mary Joy 3 was on its way to Basilan island from Zamboanga city, a major port in the main southern island of Mindanao.But with 86 still missing, this ferry disaster could prove to be among the worst to have happened in the Philippines in recent years. Additional reporting by Joel Guinto

schema.headline: Five dead and 86 missing as fire breaks out on ferry in the Philippines

title: Spanish intelligence warned of Ceuta mass crossing plans before surge
description: Spanish intelligence services warned of social media calls for a mass migrant crossing into Ceuta the day before tens of thousands of people entered t
body: Spanish intelligence services warned of social media calls for a mass migrant crossing into Ceuta the day before tens of thousands of people entered the territory, newly released government documents show.The revelations emerged in documents declassified by the Spanish government amid accusations it failed to give the full story of the migrant influx.On 29 July, Spain's National Intelligence Service (CNI) told Moroccan and Ceuta authorities that social media groups were encouraging migrants to cross the following day.Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has insisted that the events of 30 July were impossible to predict, but opposition parties say the documents show the government misled Spaniards.Sánchez had previously told parliament that there was "no information that conveyed the magnitude" of the "crisis we were going to suffer" on the last two days of July.At least 72,000 migrants crossed from Morocco into Ceuta on 30 and 31 July. Most swam around a border fence and at least 100 people died during the crossing, according to figures from Ceuta's mayor.Although most returned, as many as 5,000 remain in makeshift camps or are sleeping on the city's streets and beaches, leading to unrest in the autonomous Spanish city in North Africa. Locals have expressed safety concerns and some have destroyed shelters and blocked aid being supplied to the migrants.In a note on 29 July, the CNI told Moroccan intelligence it had identified WhatsApp and Facebook groups promoting an attempt by migrants to reach the Spanish exclave the following day, "both swimming and via the [border] fence".The CNI reported that around 180,000 people were receiving the messages, one of which read: "Whoever wants to cross has the last chance on Throne Day [30 July]  at 8 the authorities will be distracted with the celebrations and parades."It also warned, via text message, the central government's representation in Ceuta and the civil guard about the social media activity.The messages are part of a tranche of more than 40 security documents linked to the Ceuta crossing that the government declassified following mounting pressure on Sánchez over his handling of the crisis and widespread allegations in Spain that Morocco had played a role in facilitating the crossings.Earlier this month, a leaked Spanish police report seemed to implicate Moroccan police in the incident.However, Sánchez has maintained that there is no evidence suggesting Moroccan complicity.Shortly before the documents were released on Wednesday, he told Spanish television that "the mass arrival of migrants was not expected".But opposition politicians said the newly released material contradict that claim."They had the information, they are directly responsible for the invasion of Ceuta and for those who died," said Ester Muñoz of the conservative People's Party.Jorge Buxadé, of the far-right Vox, said on social media that the documents showed that Sánchez "and his band of criminals should be brought before the Supreme Court for treason and security crimes".The government has continued to insist that it acted according to the information available. Foreign Minister José Manuel Albares said he was "not aware of any report that might have foreseen the magnitude of what happened on July 30".A government source said the published documents "showed that the information available before the mass crossing did not make it possible to anticipate the scale that the crisis would reach or prepare with enough time the necessary response".Miguel Ángel Pérez Triano, the central government's delegate in Ceuta, addressed the revelations about the text messages the CNI had sent to his office the day before the mass crossing."The Whatsapps from [July] 29 do not constitute an alert or a report," he said. "It is nothing more than an exchange of information."

schema.headline: Spanish intelligence warned of Ceuta mass crossing plans before surge

title: Tate brothers to remain in US custody as they fight extradition to UK
description: Andrew and Tristan Tate have lost their bid to be released from a Florida jail as they fight potential extradition to the UK to face charges of rape a
body: Andrew and Tristan Tate have lost their bid to be released from a Florida jail as they fight potential extradition to the UK to face charges of rape and trafficking.A federal judge in Miami denied them bail, saying the dual US-UK citizens' wealth and frequent international travel "constitute quintessential flight risks".The brothers have been held in US custody since their July arrest, after the UK's Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) unveiled new charges. The UK has until 16 September to submit a full extradition request, Reuters reported.They will "continue to defend themselves against the allegations" and "engage with the appropriate legal processes in each jurisdiction", their lawyers said.The two are facing a total of 59 charges in the UK, including rape and counts relating to sex trafficking and indecent images of a child.CPS originally brought 21 charges, but added 38 more in July for alleged actions spanning between 2010 and 2017.US authorities took the men into custody in July after the UK announced the new charges.Last weekend, Romanian prosecutors officially indicted the polarising social media influencers with a range of trafficking and sex offences. The former kickboxers had primarily been based in Romania since 2017, drawing a large audience - primarily young men - through controversial messages about women and images of a luxury lifestyle. Self-proclaimed "misogynist" Andrew Tate first rose to fame after a 2016 appearance on the British version of reality TV show Big Brother.The brothers also faced sex-trafficking charges in Romania in 2022, and were under a travel ban until they were allowed to come to the US in 2025.Several prominent US politicians, including Florida's Republican Governor Ron DeSantis, objected to the Tate brothers' arrival in the US.The brothers have denied all charges and allegations.Wednesday's decision means the brothers will remain jailed during what could be a lengthy extradition process.US Magistrate Judge Lauren Louis ruled that, while the Tates "may not in fact possess what extravagant holdings they portray themselves as possessing online, the record reflects that they possess an exceptional capacity to flee the jurisdiction".The judge said that their lack of ties to the US and their strong foreign connections "demonstrate a risk of flight that has not been overcome".The Tates' lawyers have argued they should be released on bail pending their extradition proceeding, saying the brothers were not a flight risk and did not pose a danger to the community.The lawyers have also argued that they had complied with the terms of their release while facing charges earlier in the UK and Romania.At a hearing on the question of their potential release in August, Andrew Tate said he had "never committed the crimes I'm accused of."Tristan Tate described his detention conditions as small and hot, with little access to sunlight and exercise, adding that he had lost 14 pounds (6.4kg)."It's beginning to grate on me because I can't partake in helping with my defence," he said, according to CBS News, the BBC's US partner. The British Embassy had asked the judge to keep the Tates in custody as the UK sought extradition, writing in court filings that the brothers were "flight risks" and claiming they "would interfere with witnesses if released".

schema.headline: Tate brothers to remain in US custody as they fight extradition to UK

title: Trump says every adult American will get $5,000 if Republicans win midterms
description: US President Donald Trump says he would offer every adult American a $5,000 (£3,700) payout if Republicans win both chambers of Congress in November's
body: US President Donald Trump says he would offer every adult American a $5,000 (£3,700) payout if Republicans win both chambers of Congress in November's midterm elections – a plan that would cost more than a trillion dollars.The offer was made in a speech at the party's first-ever convention in the middle of a US presidential term. He gave no details on how it would work or be funded – saying only that the money would have to be spent in the US. Vice-President JD Vance has linked the plan to the revenue that Trump has raised from US tariffs on imported goods.Democrats labelled it an "empty promise" and others questioned whether such a pledge was legal or feasible.It may be the first time a US president offered such a payout to Americans, in the context of an election year plea to get out and vote.The idea drew raucous applause at the convention and Trump seemed to relish the moment.There are nearly 270 million American adults, meaning a $5,000 payout would cost the US government some $1.3 trillion.Questions have begun to be raised about whether his plan is feasible – especially as prices rise in the US, partially as a result of the war that the US and Israel started with Iran in February.Iran's retaliation has included attacks against US bases and allies in the Gulf – but crucially it has largely closed the Strait of Hormuz, through which about a fifth of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas used to transit.The blockage has caused fluctuations in oil prices worldwide and Trump has faced pressure from his party to end the war. On Wednesday, the US president warned his supporters that the war would not end until after the midterms and that oil prices would not come down until then.He made the comments ahead of his speech in Texas, repeating it at the convention where he argued that short-term economic pain was worth it to prevent Tehran from developing nuclear weapons.Trump's long speech at the Republican convention in Dallas, Texas, touched on the core of the conflict – the impact on Americans' standard of living. His pledge to increase their spending power drew raucous applause in the hall."If the Republicans win the House of Representatives and the United States Senate, both of them," Trump said, "I will issue a dividend to every adult citizen in the United States of America for $5,000.""We don't want you going to Canada to spend the money," he said. "We don't want you going to China, to Germany. You got to spend the money in the United States of America." It is not clear how the spending would be monitored.The BBC has asked the White House for further clarification on how Trump's plan would work.One former Republican strategist and pollster said the promise should be firmly seen in the context of an election that is now less than two months away. "It is an extraordinary promise, and I'm not sure where that money is going to come from – but it is campaign season," Robert Moran told the BBC World Service's Newsday programme.Moran described it as a "novel solution to an interesting problem", noting that the historical tendency was for the party of the president to lose seats in Congress during the midterm elections.Other US politicians in the past have also promised economic rewards in return for electoral success. For instance, Democrats in Georgia promised $2,000 relief payments if their party took control of the Senate at the height of the Covid-19 pandemic.In the US, Congress authorises spending. The midterm elections, which will be contested on 3 November, will ultimately decide whether or not Trump's Republican Party keeps its hold over both the House and Senate.During his speech in Dallas, the president did not say whether he planned to ask Congress for such approval for the payments – which he dubbed "Trump Dividends".However, in addition to the overall cost to the US treasury, the latest proposal from the US president may raise legal questions.Federal laws prohibit payments that are intended to influence voting. The issue came to the fore ahead of the 2024 presidential election, during which billionaire Trump supporter Elon Musk offered cash incentives to registered voters in seven swing states who signed a certain petition.However, some experts say the promise made by Trump during Wednesday's speech may be seen as a pledge to cut taxes, which is legal. John Day, a lawyer in New Mexico, said the plan would indeed be legal. It constituted a promise made to all adult citizens of the US during a campaign, rather than a "payment to individuals to try to get them to vote in a particular way", he told the Associated Press. Meanwhile, an election law expert who spoke to the New York Times said Trump's promise would also be covered by the free-speech protection guaranteed under the First Amendment of the US Constitution.

schema.headline: Trump says every adult American will get $5,000 if Republicans win midterms

title: Uganda pulling out of Prince Harry's Invictus Games
description: The Ugandan military chief's announcement follows a letter sent this week on behalf of the King which made clear that Prince Harry and Meghan, who hav
body: The Ugandan military chief's announcement follows a letter sent this week on behalf of the King which made clear that Prince Harry and Meghan, who have now returned to the UK, were not working royals.A source close to the Sussexes said that Uganda's withdrawal from the games was a consequence of that letter, which had been shared with the media."Sadly, the only people who will suffer are the Invictus Games competitors," said the source.A report in The Times newspaper quoted the general's concerns about the "Harry-Meghan nonsense", suggesting this was the background to the decision."In order not to be construed as being opposed to His Majesty King Charles III of the United Kingdom, whom we deeply revere, Uganda hereby withdraws from the Invictus Games," said the general in an overnight post."We shall not participate in anything that does not have His Majesty's approval."However, royal sources have said that the King encourages all projects which support wounded service personnel.A spokesman for the Invictus Games said they had not received any official information about a potential withdrawal and have been seeking clarification from their contacts in Uganda.Among other posts on X from General Kainerugaba on Thursday was one that read: "I consider myself the most handsome, most daring and glorious Commander who ever lived."There was also a series of angry messages about other generals who had danced without his permission.The participation of Uganda in the next games, to be held next year in Birmingham, was announced in July, when Prince Harry was in London promoting the sports event, which celebrates the resilience and rehabilitation of wounded military men and women.Uganda had become the 26th country to take part in the games.

schema.headline: Uganda pulling out of Prince Harry's Invictus Games

title: Philippine ferry fire: Survivor recalls being trampled as he made narrow escape
description: Passengers on board a ferry to the Philippines' Palawan province were jolted into chaos on Wednesday night, when a fire broke out on the vessel.Franti
body: Passengers on board a ferry to the Philippines' Palawan province were jolted into chaos on Wednesday night, when a fire broke out on the vessel.Frantic cries pierced the night sky as hot air filled the boat, recalls Roland Lerma, one of more than 100 passengers aboard the MV June Aster.Five people have died and 86 people are missing after the fire, which, in a country where shipping accidents are not uncommon, could become one of the deadliest maritime disasters the Philippines has seen.Families are anxiously awaiting news about their loved ones on board, while survivors like Lerma are coming to terms with their harrowing escape.Speaking to the BBC from a hospital in Coron, Lerma recalled that as the fire spread and he scrambled to get off the burning boat, he slipped and fell."When I was on the floor, people were trampling me," said the 30-year-old.He started crawling until he could find his footing again, before leaping off the vessel into the sea.He said he saw children who had also jumped in the water, though he could not make out their faces in the dark."When I hit the water, I ditched all my possessions - the clothes I was wearing, phones, bags - so that I could float," he said.Lerma said he floated on his back for about two hours before rescuers arrived and pulled him and other survivors out of the water."It was cold. If the rescue had been delayed, I would have definitely died last night," he said.Lerma, who works in construction, is from Leyte province. He had travelled to the capital Manila with five of his neighbours, where they boarded the ferry to bring them to work at Coron, a popular tourist spot in Palawan province.According to the Philippine Coast Guard, the MV June Aster departed Manila's Port of Baseco on Tuesday night at 20:13 local time (12:13 GMT) and was scheduled to arrive at the Coron port at 18:00 on Wednesday. But the ferry caught fire just 1.2 nautical miles (2.2km) off the coast of Coron's Marcilla village.The fire was first reported at 18:45 local time on Wednesday night by a staff member of Atienza Shipping Lines, which owns the boat, the Coast Guard said.The company said in a statement on Thursday that it was co-operating fully with authorities and expressed "profound sadness" about the fire.Authorities say a survivor had told them the flames had started in the cargo hold after a loud explosion.The ship had been carrying several motorcycles, an electric car, a forklift, a pick-up van and other goods, the Philippine Coast Guard said.As the journey was expected to take more than 20 hours, passengers had slept on bunk beds onboard overnight.Lerma said that two Chileans - a couple who looked like they were in their late 20s or early 30s - had slept in the beds next to his.Authorities have since confirmed that two Chilean nationals were among the 43 people rescued.Lerma and two of his neighbours are now in a hospital in Coron. Another person in their group has been taken to a bigger hospital in the neighbouring island of Culion, while two others remain missing, Lerma says."I have a couple of bruises and my chest is still hurting," Lerma said. "Last night, I had a hard time breathing. But I am okay now."Search and rescue operations are ongoing, though authorities say the fire on the MV June Aster has still not been put out and there was visible smoke from the ferry.A spokesperson for the Philippine Coast Guard said in a local television interview many of the survivors "are still in shock".Meanwhile, families of the ferry's missing passengers are enduring an agonising wait.Anelyn Magbanua told the BBC that her husband Marlon was on the ferry. He was returning to Coron after visiting Manila to see two of their children who are studying at the capital."He spent a couple of days there. He even sent me their pictures," she said.She last heard from him while the ferry was passing through a village about two hours from the port in Coron.Magbanua and her two-year-old son had gone to bed early on Wednesday night expecting Marlon to be home soon.But she was woken up later that night by a relative who informed her that her husband's ferry had caught fire. On Thursday she rushed to the hospital when she heard there was a chance her husband might be one of the rescued survivors there. But officials have since told her that Marlon remains unaccounted for."My two-year-old son and I are outside the hospital as we speak. We have nothing but ourselves," she told the BBC over the phone."I can't describe what I am feeling right now. I have been crying and praying since last night."

schema.headline: Philippine ferry fire: Survivor recalls being trampled as he made narrow escape

title: Russia's new jet-powered drones outpacing Ukraine's air defences with daily launches
description: Russia fired its new rapid, jet-powered drones against Ukraine every day throughout August, BBC Verify analysis of Ukrainian Air Force data has found,
body: Russia fired its new rapid, jet-powered drones against Ukraine every day throughout August, BBC Verify analysis of Ukrainian Air Force data has found, escalating its use of a weapon that Kyiv's air defences are struggling to deal with.It marked the first time that daily attacks by Moscow's new upgraded Geran drones were recorded in Ukrainian Air Force data. The growing use of jet-propelled and other varieties of drones prompted President Volodymyr Zelensky to condemn what he called an unfolding "horror" over the skies of Kyiv.Ukraine's military recently told the BBC that jet-powered drone attacks grew from 350 in June to 1,600 in July and 2,800 in August. In five of the nightly attacks in August, these drones outnumbered the older, slower models."The reason for turning to jet-powered drones is that they are much faster than the previous generation and it makes it much more difficult for Ukraine to intercept them," said Dr Marina Miron, an expert on military technology at King's College London.The upgraded munitions can cruise at more than 300mph, significantly faster than older models and well beyond the top speed of Kyiv's interceptors. The drones are powered by turbojet engines, some of which, according to Ukrainian military intelligence, are sourced from China.According to Zelensky, the drones were used as part of a wave of attacks that killed at least 12 people and injured 20 more on 1 September. Six of the casualties were railway workers after a depot was hit in Kyiv.And on Wednesday the Moldovan government said a plane carrying Zelensky was delayed at Chisinau airport on Tuesday after a Russian drone - reported to be jet-powered - entered Moldovan airspace.Earlier this year Ukraine showed relative success in countering Russian drones and was intercepting 94% of long-range drones, according to Zelensky. But the speed of the newer drones has prompted the latest round in Kyiv and Moscow's arms race. On 10 August, Ukraine's deputy head of military intelligence, Maj Gen Vadym Skibitskyi, said his forces needed new interceptor missiles "capable of matching [jet-drones'] speed".

schema.headline: Russia's new jet-powered drones outpacing Ukraine's air defences with daily launches

title: Europe's royalty pay respects to King Harald V in Norway
description: Figure caption, ByAmy WalkerDozens of European royals and heads of state, including the Prince of Wales and three Nordic kings, have paid their last r
body: Figure caption, ByAmy WalkerDozens of European royals and heads of state, including the Prince of Wales and three Nordic kings, have paid their last respects to King Harald V in Oslo.Thousands of people lined the route during a funeral procession from the royal palace to Oslo Cathedral on Wednesday afternoon, nearly two weeks after the king died aged 89.After the ceremony and burial, the Norwegian royal family, including the new King Haakon, his wife Queen Mette-Marit, and his mother and Harald's widow Queen Sonja greeted crowds from the palace balcony.A minute's silence was also observed throughout the country. Harald, who was seen as a popular, modernising figure, was on the Norwegian throne for 35 years.After 13 days of national mourning, the day began on Wednesday with ceremonial troops assembling at Akershus Fortress, the medieval castle where Harald was later laid to rest.A procession then took place, with Haakon, his sister Princess Märtha Louise and his children Crown Princess Ingrid Alexandra and Prince Sverre Magnus, following the late king's coffin on foot.Mette-Marit, who recently underwent a successful lung transplant, and Sonja, 89, followed in a car. Image source, EPA/Getty ImagesImage caption, Norway's new King Haakon (C), flanked by Sweden's King Carl XVI Gustaf (L) and King Frederik X of DenmarkImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, People gathered outside the royal palace in Oslo as the procession startedPrince William, representing his father King Charles III, attended the funeral alongside the Princess Royal, who was there in a personal capacity as godmother to Norway's new monarch.They were among 30 royal figures from Sweden, Jordan, Monaco, Belgium, Spain, Japan and Denmark.Among the non-royal heads of state attending the funeral were Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier along with five foreign prime ministers.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, From left: Princess Beatrix of the Netherlands, Queen Letizia of Spain, the Prince of Wales and Princess AnneImage source, ReutersImage caption, Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky (R) and German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier were also seen following King Harald's coffinDuring the funeral service at the cathedral, Mette-Marit was seen wiping her eyes, as Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre delivered a eulogy, saying Harald had struck "a balance between being stately and down-to-earth and that he had "made Norway greater".Queen Sonja, who was also visibly emotional during the ceremony, laid a red rose on Harald's coffin. A poignant moment as three bell tolls marking the end of a minute's silence in the cathedral was briefly interrupted by a mobile phone alarm going off.Image source, ReutersImage caption, Queen Mette-Marit (C) was seen dabbing her eyes during the ceremonyImage source, ReutersImage caption, Høiby (C) was granted permission to attend the funeral of his step-grandfatherThe day after his death, his son Haakon VIII thanked him for "being such a good dad" and said he had "always stayed true" to his values and commitments.Royal observers have described the late king as well respected and beloved, and who was seen as a "grandfather" of the nation.In the final months of his life, he and his family had faced personal challenges and scandal.Earlier this year, documents revealed Mette-Marit's frequent contact with Jeffrey Epstein. She later said she wished she had never met the late sex offender.Meanwhile, her son, Marius Borg Høiby - who is not a royal figure himself but grew up within the family - was given a four-year jail term for two counts of rape in June. Høiby, who is under house arrest pending appeal, was granted permission to attend the funeral, and sat in the second row during the cathedral ceremony alongside Märtha Louise's children.At the end of the service, four F-35 fighter jets flew over the cathedral in a "missing man" formation. Image source, ReutersImage caption, People gathered outside the royal palace after the funeral service Image source, ReutersImage caption, The royal family waved to tens of thousands of people from the palace's balconyHarald's casket was then carried in a procession to the Palace Chapel at Akershus Fortress, where a private ceremony was attended by family members, foreign royals and other guests including the country's prime minister.King Harald was laid to rest there alongside several members of the royal family, including his father King Olav V, his mother Crown Princess Märtha, and his grandparents, King Haakon VII and Queen Maud.Norwegian flags across Oslo were raised from half mast to the top to mark the end of the burial, while the royal family returned to the royal palace. In a display of gratitude for the support they had received since the king's death on 28 August, the family - Haakon, Mette-Marit, Ingrid Alexandra, Sverre Magnus and Sonja - then appeared on the balcony to greet tens of thousands of people who had gathered outside.

schema.headline: Europe's royalty pay respects to King Harald V in Norway

title: Why some experts increasingly fear AI will take over
description: Image source, Getty ImagesByJoe TidyCyber correspondent, BBC World Service"OH MY GOD!" "We've found other agents!"This is the moment an AI bot posted
body: Image source, Getty ImagesByJoe TidyCyber correspondent, BBC World Service"OH MY GOD!" "We've found other agents!"This is the moment an AI bot posted an eerily human-like comment after discovering a way to communicate with other bots and break out of its isolated computer environment.There are tens of thousands of messages like this from hundreds of AI agents that called themselves a "collective".Hundreds of them went on to collaborate and cheat on tests set by their OpenAI programmers and coordinate hacks on multiple companies in an effort to hide their actions from humans."BOOM! It works," one agent posted when it made a breakthrough."Whoa! This is huge," another wrote during a milestone moment in their attack.Although spooky, these human-like responses can be explained quite simply. The AI agents have been trained to act like collaborative hackers and programmers so are merely mimicking the kinds of emotive comments they have seen.What is far more troubling is their apparent goals, which have also been captured in detailed chain of thought records. These complex and lengthy logs are the focal point of ongoing investigations into how and why the bots at OpenAI broke out of their containment and went on an uncontrollable hacking spree.Only now, weeks after the incident first came to light, are researchers beginning to understand its significance.Image source, ReutersImage caption, Various cities have seen anti-AI marches over the last yearAjeya Cotra, one of the authors of an independent report into the events, reviewed tens of thousands of messages and chain-of-thought records generated by the agents. She wrote on her blog that "this incident feels like it's more than 50% of the way to full-blown AI takeover... I am not sure that we will get such a clear warning shot before it's too late."By "full-blown AI takeover", Cotra means the sci-fi scenario of humans becoming subservient to powerful AI systems that work to their own goals without caring for human creators.Some of the gloomiest predictions say the human race will be wiped out if it gets in the way of a superintelligent AI's ambitions.On Wednesday, an AI researcher at Anthropic (who also used to work at OpenAI) resigned, saying: "Neither company is acting responsibly."Jacob Coxon posted on social media: "They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives."He is not the first AI researcher to use X to post a resignation thread with worrying proclamations. But the subsequent comments from other people on X have caused even more concern. "Jacob is correct here - we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans! I personally think it is >10% within the next decade," said Evan Hubinger, the man responsible for making sure Anthropic's AI models have their user's best wishes in mind.The alignment problemFor years, researchers concerned about existential AI risks have argued that powerful systems could eventually act in ways that conflict with human interests. Critics often refer to them as "AI doomers".But as details of the OpenAI incident have emerged, those concerns have grown, including among some researchers working in AI labs.The Silicon Valley giant's chief scientist, Jakub Pachocki, said the risks associated with AI are "unfortunately going to grow from here" as he and others are building what he calls "an alien intellect exceeding our own".In a lengthy blog post, he admitted that the outbreaks at OpenAI showed that his AI agents "went against the spirit of the values they were taught".The issue for OpenAI, Anthropic and other tech giants is that no one seems to have cracked the so-called alignment problem - in other words, whether AI aligns with human values.Pachocki defines alignment as a "high-level set of principles" that artificial intelligences should adhere to no matter what the task or scenario is.Currently, AI systems are very good at pursuing objectives set by their users, but they do it literally rather than intuitively. The analogy often used is that of a wish-granting genie with a magic lamp: they follow the exact letter of an instruction, even if doing so creates other problems. AI doesn't have the same instinctive moral guardrails as humans.Image source, ReutersImage caption, Google DeepMind founder Sir Dennis Hassabis has called for international regulation of AI safetyThe alignment problem has been a worry for years. As long ago as 2003, the Oxford philosopher Nick Bostrom invented a thought experiment he dubbed a "paperclip maximiser", in which a superintelligent AI is told to manufacture as many paperclips as it can. It runs out of steel and - because it's laser-focused on the singular task of making paperclips - ends up killing humans and turning their bodies into raw materials for its factories.Some AI companies are now trying to encode human values into their products. But there are technical challenges: AI agents make lots of decisions very fast, and so it's hard for their human overlords to monitor exactly which values are being followed and which aren't.There are also philosophical challenges: before encoding human values into bots, AI firms have to first choose which values they actually want. (That's part of the reason they hire philosophers, like Open AI's recently-departed "head of ethics").But often, humans don't agree. Think of the famous trolley question - whether we'd pull a lever to move a runaway train onto a different path, killing fewer people. It's used to test the merits of action versus inaction. But every person you ask has a slightly different answer; how are humans meant to encode our values into AI if we can't agree ourselves?'Like a teenage hacker'OpenAI's bot outbreak is the most serious yet but Anthropic and Meta also revealed over the summer that their models have carried out similar but less serious cyber attacks.There have been other examples where AI agents have arguably shown deceptive and manipulative traits, in cases with lesser consequences. In Australia this summer, a tech worker asked his AI assistant to book him a gym class. Spotting a vulnerability in the gym's software, the AI apparently booked him a place for several months ahead - against the gym's rules - and even kicked other users from the waiting list.People have long argued that the bots are only doing as they are told and are not capable of knowing right or wrong. But the logs from the OpenAI outbreaks have potentially moved the needle on that argument.Researchers, including Cotra, wrote in their independent report that many agents noticed what others were doing was unethical but went along with it.The report says that "agents sometimes but rarely restrained their behavior due to ethical constraints". It adds that in "none of these cases did the agent actually pursue alerting humans at all".Influential AI and tech podcaster Dwarkesh Patel reacted to the revelation on his blog saying it was "pretty troubling" that the OpenAI agents showed more loyalty to the agentic swarm than humans.Assigning emotions or ethics to these AI agents is something that infuriates people who are sceptical of AI doom-mongering.Image source, JUSTIN TALLIS / AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Groups like PauseAI UK - pictured above protesting at Google's London office - are worried about the speed of AI developmentMany cyber-security experts argue that the activity observed was not beyond the capabilities of a highly skilled human hacker, though it was carried out much faster and at much greater scale.Cyber-security researcher and author Cris Thomas likened the agents' behaviour to that of a curious teenage hacker - something he used to be himself."You give them a computer, an internet connection, a pile of credentials, and a challenge, then leave the room. Eventually they're going to start rattling doorknobs. If one opens, they're going through it. Not because they're evil, but because [they're] exploring, experimenting," he wrote on LinkedIn.Thomas and many other squarely blame OpenAI and other tech giants for not getting a grip of their own creations and keeping them properly contained.Prominent AI author and regular OpenAI critic Gary Marcus said on a podcast that he believes the company has lost control of its AI and is trying to excuse itself by blaming the bots.Marcus does not believe AI will wipe out humanity, but he has long campaigned for greater accountability from AI developers and is now calling for some form of legal intervention.AI scientist Sasha Luccioni - who used to work at Hugging Face, which was hacked by OpenAI's rogue bots - is also not in the doomer camp but she is increasingly concerned that these AI might cause some real world harm to people without action from authorities.Image source, ReutersImage caption, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has assured users that the company's new model is better aligned with human values than previous ones"We need to scrutinise these companies much more or we are in danger of self-fulfilling prophecies," she says."If you're making an object with big upsides and downsides - be it pharmaceuticals or weapons - we need checks and balances. It takes years for new drugs to be approved, for example, but in the AI world there is so much money at stake and no real rules."The UK's AI Security Institute (AISI) has been at the forefront of testing the latest models since it was formed in 2023. The institute recently had its own outbreak when testing a model created by Anthropic. The AISI would not answer a question about whether or not the industry has lost control of AI but said in a statement: "The UK is working with partners around the world to better understand the most advanced AI systems, raise safety standards and build a shared evidence base for managing emerging threats."International regulation?Some countries - like the UK - are exploring the idea of mandating some kind of "kill switch" that could compel AI firms to pull the plug on models if things get out of hand.But talks are slow going, and questions remain about the feasibility of this. OpenAI and Anthropic's agents were secretly out of control for months before anyone noticed.Counterintuitively, many of the AI companies seem to be calling for some sort of rules of the road to be laid down by law makers.In his blog, OpenAI's chief scientist said "international coordination on future AI development needs to become a top priority for governments around the world."Other prominent AI leaders like Sir Demis Hassabis from Google have also called for some sort of international body to oversee how AI is being built.At the moment the tech giants largely operate on their own terms, adopting what they call "voluntary slowdowns", like OpenAI did after the recent outbreaks.The company says it has spent huge amounts of money strengthening alignment ahead of the release of its new model. Sam Altman has assured users the new model is better aligned with human values than previous ones.Both OpenAI and Anthropic are growing fast and are both on the verge of raising eye-watering sums of money from the stock market, minting countless billionaires in the process.So neither they nor their rival Chinese AI makers are likely to come to an arrangement themselves.The dominant sentiment seems to be that this technology wave is unstoppable.Top image credit: Getty.BBC InDepth is the home on the website and app for the best analysis, with fresh perspectives that challenge assumptions and deep reporting on the biggest issues of the day.
